analysis.one_liner: Keeps medical bills off credit reports for one year and erases paid-off medical debt.
analysis.headline: The Medical Debt Relief Act won 48 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee markup or a House vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how medical bills show up in your credit file. Credit bureaus could not put a medical debt on a credit report until it is at least a year old, so people would have time to settle bills, dispute charges, or get insurance or hospital charity care to cover them. Once a medical debt was paid or settled, it would have to come off the report within 45 days. Debt collectors would also have to send you a written notice before reporting a medical debt, including the exact date reporting could begin. The bill was introduced in February 2021 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, and it never came to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 100 million Americans who carry medical debt, and especially people who are disputing a bill, waiting on an insurance decision, or eligible for hospital financial assistance. A single medical bill in collections can drop a credit score enough to raise the cost of a car loan, an apartment rental, or a mortgage for years. This bill would give people a one-year window to resolve bills before the damage hits their credit, and it would wipe paid-off medical debts off reports almost immediately instead of letting them linger up to seven years.

how_it_helps.text: Credit bureaus could not report a medical debt until one year after it went to collection, giving patients time to resolve it with insurers or hospital assistance programs first.
A fully paid or settled medical debt would have to come off a credit report within 45 days, instead of staying on for years.

Before reporting a medical debt, a collector would have to send the patient a notice stating that the debt cannot be reported for a year, the specific date reporting could start, and that paying or settling during that window would keep it off the report entirely.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus, which would lose a category of data they sell to lenders, and debt collection firms, which use the threat of credit damage to push people to pay quickly. Medical providers would lose some of the leverage that credit reporting gives them to press patients for payment, though they could still pursue and collect the debt itself.

drawbacks.text: Lenders would lose a year of information about borrowers' unpaid medical debts, which some argue makes credit pricing less accurate and could raise borrowing costs for everyone. (Studies have found medical debt is a weak predictor of default, which is the counterargument.)

The bill does not reduce what people owe. A hospital or collector could still pursue payment through calls, letters, and lawsuits during the one-year waiting period; it only delays the credit report hit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and large for the people affected: credit damage from medical bills, unlike most debt, often reflects bad insurance coverage or billing disputes rather than a failure to pay, and the bill's waiting period targets exactly that gap. The cost is a modest loss of information for lenders and a slower path to pressure patients to pay. The most honest criticism is that it treats a symptom: people would still owe the money, and the bill does nothing about the underlying medical prices or insurance gaps that create the debt in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a markup or vote on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the Medical Debt Relief Act of 2021 on February 3, 2021, with 47 Democratic cosponsors signing on the same day.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, which was its only action of the Congress.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote on the bill appears in the action history before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill would have barred consumer reporting agencies from including medical debts less than a year old on credit reports and required removal of paid or settled medical debts after 45 days.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and debt collection companies kept the status quo: they can continue reporting medical bills to credit reports immediately and keep paid-off medical debt on file for years. Patients with medical debt continue to absorb the credit score damage that the bill would have delayed or erased.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 supporters were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it never advanced far enough to produce a roll-call vote.

industries.note: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion would lose a category of data they currently collect and sell to lenders, including medical debts that have already been paid. Consumers would regain access to credit on fairer terms because a paid medical bill could no longer haunt their file for years.

Collectors use the threat of credit damage to push people to pay quickly; the one-year waiting period and mandatory notice would remove that leverage for medical bills, though collectors could still pursue the debt by other means.

Providers could still bill and sue for unpaid care, but they would lose the immediate credit-reporting threat that pressures patients to pay before insurance disputes are resolved. Patients would gain a year to pursue coverage or hospital financial assistance first.
